In medieval Latin-script writing, ⟨u⟩ and ⟨v⟩ were positional forms of a single letter; they later became distinct letters, with ⟨u⟩ used for the vowel. / The uppercase form of u. From Latin V, as a later rounded graphic variant of the same letter, from an Old Italic form of Ancient Greek Υ (U, “upsilon”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤅 (w, “waw; hook”), from Proto-Canaanite , from Proto-Sinaitic , from Egyptian 𓌉 representing a mace.
In Latin, ⟨V⟩ originally represented both the vowel /u/ and the consonant /w/; the distinct letterforms ⟨U⟩ and ⟨V⟩ became conventional from the 16th century.

en.g: Libya; Africa, especially the region west of the Nile, as named in ancient Greek geography; see Oldtidens Libya
x: I oldtidsgresk geografi kunne Libya betegne hele Afrika.
In ancient Greek geography, Libya could denote the whole of Africa.
Libya, eller Libye, var navnet som oldtidens grekere brukte på Afrika.
Libya, or Libye, was the name used by the ancient Greeks for Africa.

1000020.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Latin Libya, from Ancient Greek Λιβύη (Libúē). The Ancient Greek name is based on the ethnonym of the Libu, a North African people whose name is attested in Egyptian as rbw (“Libu; Libya”) and later in Punic as 𐤋𐤁𐤉 (lby). The immediate transmission route into Norwegian is unknown.
In ancient Greek geography, the name originally referred to the land west of the Nile and was later extended to Africa as a whole. The modern state name revives this ancient geographical name; Tripolitania, Cyrenaica and Fezzan were brought together under Italian colonial administration und

1001044.etyen:
From hisse (“to excite, incite; stir up”) + -ing (“action/result-forming noun suffix”). The base verb represents a merger of two historically distinct verbs; see hisse for the full historical development.
Compare the parallel formation Swedish hetsning (“incitement, agitation”).

1001300.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Arni m, originally a short form of compound names whose first element meant “eagle”, from ǫrn (“eagle”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *arô (“eagle”).
Cognate with Faroese Árni, Icelandic Árni, Danish Arne and Swedish Arne.

en.g: a surname originating as a patronymic, originally meaning “son of Anders”

1001556.etyen:
From Anders (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Anders”. The given name Anders is a Nordic form of Ἀνδρέας (Andréas, “male given name”), derived from ἀνδρεῖος (andreîos, “manly, brave”).
Compare Danish Andersen, Swedish Andersson and English Anderson.

1004628.etyen:
From bestemor (“grandmother”) + stang (“pole, rod”). Apparently so called because its traditional design—a round wooden pole with decorative wall fittings and end knobs—was associated with the type of curtain rod found in a grandmother's home.
Compare oldemorstang (“curtain rod of the same traditional type”) and Swedish mormorsstång (“curtain rod of the same traditional type”).

en.g: thankfully, fortunately, thank God; used to express relief or gratitude about the situation described
x: Vi hadde gudskjetakk en ekstra nøkkel.
Thankfully, we had a spare key.

1005140.etyen:
Univerbation of Gud (“God”) + skje (“to be accorded”) + takk (“thanks”), from the expression gud skje takk, literally “thanks be to God”. Here skje retains the older sense “be accorded, fall to”.
The first element continues Old Norse guð (“God, god”), also goð, from Proto-Germanic *gudą (“god”); its further origin is disputed. The verb derives from Middle Low German schēn (“to happen”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skehaną (“to move quickly; happen”), from Proto-Indo-European *skek- (“to move quickly, jump”). The final element continues Old Norse þǫkk (“thanks, gratitude”), from Proto-Germa
